did_you_know.text: The phrase “heaven and earth” is a biblical way of referring to the whole world, not only the sky and the ground.
The word bohu is very rare in the Bible, appearing only three times, always in descriptions of emptiness or desolation.
The order “evening and morning” is repeated throughout the chapter and is connected to the Jewish tradition that a day begins in the evening.
The word rakia describes an expanse stretched above the earth, so translations use words such as dome, expanse, or firmament.
The word moadim can mean appointed times, and in the Bible it is also used for festivals and sacred occasions.
The word sheretz does not name one particular animal; it describes small or numerous creatures that swarm in water or move across the land.
The word tanninim can refer to large sea creatures and elsewhere in the Bible to serpents or monsters; here they are presented simply as created beings.
The wording “Let us make humankind” is plural, and it has inspired different interpretations, such as an address to a heavenly council or a royal plural.
The verse emphasizes that both male and female are created in the image of God, so that image does not belong to only one sex.
Only after the entire creation is complete does the phrase “very good” appear instead of merely “good,” suggesting that the whole picture matters.
